notes:
I've written notes on all nine verses below, but the research is incomplete. My search and page-reading tools stopped working partway through, so I could only fully read one page (Enduring Word). Everything else comes from search-result excerpts, mostly the verse commentary collections on biblehub.com, studylight.org and blueletterbible.org. As a result:

- **Not found at all:** Catholic, Orthodox and modern-scholarship views (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com and oca.org were never reached), plus Wesley's own notes and any Lutheran or Anglican teacher.
- **Thin coverage:** verses 2–5. Verses 4–5 rest almost entirely on Enduring Word.

The Enduring Word page had no excerpt markers, so I give its URL without quotation tags.

---

**Title / v. 1**
- **Who wrote it and why (David Guzik, Enduring Word):** This is one of four Songs of Ascents credited to David. Guzik thinks David wrote it in the voice of a pilgrim, probably looking ahead to the temple Solomon would build, since in David's day there was only the tabernacle. He reads "they said" as the group and "I was glad" as the individual: corporate worship should be glad, though not the same as entertainment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** The word was not "go," but "let us go"; hence the ear of the Psalmist found a double joy in it. He also applies the verse to the Lord's Day, the church, and finally heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/122-1.htm
- **Barnes (setting):** The speaker is not known. It may have been David himself; more probably, however, it was designed by him to be used by those who should go up to worship. "House of the LORD" means the tabernacle if the psalm is from David's time, or the temple if it is later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/122-1.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** David's joy is linked to God finally choosing a fixed home for the ark. From the time of Moses, for the space of more than a thousand years, the Ark of the Covenant had been carried about from place to place... At length it was revealed to David, that mount Zion was the spot. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/122-1.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** He notes the alternative translation "I rejoiced in", or "because of, those that said unto me". He treats the tabernacle as typical of the church of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/122-1.htm
- **Clarke (Methodist):** Clarke dates the psalm after the exile: When Cyrus published an edict for their return, the very first object of their thanksgiving was the kindness of God in permitting them to return to his ordinances. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-122.html
- **Ellicott:** "Let us go" can also be translated "we will go." This verse is inscribed over the portico of St. Paul's Cathedral. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/122.htm

**v. 2**
- **Guzik:** Most read this as the glad cry of a pilgrim who has finally arrived. They came to Jerusalem because David had placed the tabernacle, the ark and the altar there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/
- **JFB:** Our feet shall stand—literally, "are standing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/122-1.htm
- **Clarke (exile reading):** For seventy years we have been exiled from our own land; our heart was in Jerusalem, but our feet were in Chaldea. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-122.html

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** Jerusalem was small but orderly, "a real city." He quotes Kidner: the Hebrew verb for "compact" is the same one used for joining the tabernacle into one whole (Exodus 26:11). He also quotes Spurgeon's appeal for church unity ("she needs compacting, not dividing"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/
- **Ellicott (another way to read the Hebrew):** Some take "compact" as a noun meaning "union." The verse then means Jerusalem, the (one) built like a city, union is in it together, i.e., it is the rallying point of all the tribes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/122.htm
- **Clarke:** He reads the psalm as praise of the Church, under the name of Jerusalem, for her unity, Psalms 122:3; religious worship, Psalms 122:4; civil and ecclesiastical policy, Psalms 122:5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-122.html

**v. 4**
- **Guzik:**
  - Jerusalem had belonged to no tribe before David took it, so it could belong to all of them.
  - "The Testimony of Israel" (NKJV wording; the BSB has "as a testimony for Israel") means the ark of the covenant.
  - Guzik argues the mention of the ark counts against the view that the psalm dates from after the exile (Clarke's view), because the returning exiles had no ark.
  - Quoting Kidner, the feasts existed to give thanks, not mainly to gain unity or prosperity, unlike pagan worship.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:**
  - Jerusalem was the seat of the main courts, a city meant for justice.
  - These thrones of judgment may have stood at the city gates (Ruth 4).
  - David's house reigns for ever in the Messiah, the Son of David.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/
- **A Bible Hub article:** It draws the point that The throne of David (v.5) and the house of Yahweh (v.1) stand side by side—government and worship united under divine authority. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Psalm_122_6_for_Christians.htm

**v. 6**
- **Wordplay:** Spurgeon: Peace was her name, pray that her condition may verify her title. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps122.cfm. A source quoted under Calvin shows the sound-play across the Hebrew words for pray, peace, Jerusalem and prosper. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_5/psalm_122_6-9.htm
- **Clarke:** shalom signifies both peace and prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/122-6.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Pray particularly for the uniting of the inhabitants among themselves and their preservation from the incursions of enemies. He applies this to the gospel church, particularly in our land. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_122.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "They shall prosper that love thee" is A covert threat, as well as a promise. https://biblehub.com/psalms/122-6.htm
- **Calvin:** David urges God's worshippers to pray and promises that, in this way the divine blessing will descend upon them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/122-6.html

**v. 7**
- **Clarke:** This is the actual wording of the prayer: peace on all the people within the walls, and calm especially in the dwellings of thy princes and rulers (Benson, following the same line). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/122-6.htm
- **Henry:** Peace be in thy fortifications; let them never be attacked, or, if they be, let them never be taken. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_122.cfm
- **Guzik, quoting Kidner:** Peace and prosperity are the natural fruits of the justice described in v. 5. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/

**v. 8**
- **Spurgeon:** It is for the good of every Christian, yea, of every man, that there should be peace and prosperity in the church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps122.cfm
- **Calvin:** David is answering any suspicion that praising Jerusalem served his own kingdom. He is driven by a concern for the whole Church, and "brethren" means all believers. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_5/psalm_122_6-9.htm
- **Clarke:** Because this city is the abode of my kinsfolk and countrymen, I will wish it prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-122.html

**v. 9**
- **Calvin:** This is the second reason: the worship of God so far from remaining entire would go to ruin unless Jerusalem continued standing. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_5/psalm_122_6-9.htm
- **Constable:** He sought the welfare of Jerusalem chiefly because the house of Yahweh stood within it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/122-6.html
- **Horne, quoted by Benson:** The two motives are love of the brothers and love of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/122-6.htm
- **Guzik, quoting G. Campbell Morgan:** It is not a song of buildings or of material magnificence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/

---

**Where readings differ (from what I found)**
- **When was it written? (vv. 1–4).** Clarke (Methodist) reads it as a song of exiles returning from Babylon (vv. 1–2, 9). Guzik argues the ark in v. 4 counts against that. Barnes stays undecided. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-122.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/
- **Jerusalem as the church (vv. 3, 6).** Gill (Baptist), Calvin (Reformed), Henry, Spurgeon and Clarke all apply "Jerusalem" to the church. Gill goes further, reading v. 6 as a prayer for the spiritual Jerusalem and for Christ's coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/122-6.html
- **Praying for the present-day city (v. 6).** Some writers press v. 6 toward the literal city, against the "church" reading:
  - The Bible Hub study note says the prayer's deepest fulfillment awaits the reign of the Messiah, the Prince of Peace, who will establish His kingdom from Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/psalms/122-6.htm
  - A Bible Hub article directly rejects the idea that the verse is obsolete because the church replaces Israel. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Psalm_122_6_for_Christians.htm
  - Everett: when we pray for the peace of Jerusalem, we are essentially praying for Jesus' Return. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/psalms-122.html
  - Guzik takes a middle line: pray for the earthly city's elusive peace, while applying the psalm to the church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-122/

**Does "prosper" mean material gain? (v. 6)**
I found no prosperity-gospel or word-of-faith teacher on this verse. The traditional sources do, however, take a position on the question:
- **Barnes:** The word prosper conveys an idea which is not in the original. He takes it to mean peace with God and peace of conscience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/122-6.htm
- **Bible Hub study note:** The prosperity in view includes spiritual well-being and participation in God's blessing, not merely material gain. https://biblehub.com/psalms/122-6.htm
- **Henry:** Those who love Zion will prosper; at least their souls shall prosper. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_122.cfm
- **Gill:** He allows for outward blessing too, giving the example of Obed-edom being blessed for keeping the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/122-6.htm
